description: We're a team of data science students from Sri Lanka taking on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our goal is to build an AI-powered tool that searches NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey for faint moving objects, going beyond what single images can show by using a "shift-and-stack" technique. Even if Planet X stays hidden, our system will map where it can't be, turning the search into real science. We love hard problems, learning new fields, and combining computer vision with space data
summary: Galadriel is a free web tool that lets anyone search NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey for things that move or change: nearby stars, cold brown dwarfs and, one day perhaps, an unknown planet. Type a star's name or coordinates and Galadriel finds every SPHEREx picture of that spot, cleans and aligns them, and plays them as a blink so moving objects jump out. Click anything to get its speed measured from SPHEREx alone, a check against ESA's Gaia catalogue, its 0.75–5 µm spectrum and its light curve. We tested it on all five challenge targets with real data: every speed lands within one SPHEREx pixel of the catalogue value. Guided missions, plain-language explanations and 10 languages, including Sinhala and Tamil, mean a school student in Colombo can join the same search as a professional astronomer.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Planet X, if it exists, would be cold and faint: invisible in visible light but glowing in the infrared, and creeping across the sky over months. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, so motion like that is in its data. The hard part is seeing it. Galadriel turns the SPHEREx archive into a "blink comparator", the technique that found Pluto in 1930, but in a web browser, for any spot on the sky.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find: a query to NASA/IPAC IRSA lists every SPHEREx image covering the target. Star names are resolved with CDS Sesame and moved to today's position using their proper motion (Barnard's Star is 4.4′ away from its year-2000 position).

2. Clean: for each image a small cutout is downloaded; the zodiacal-light model is subtracted, bad pixels are masked using the quality flags, overloaded star centres are filled, and every cutout is aligned onto one common grid.

3. Group: images are grouped into visits, stacked per visit and per camera, scaled to signal-to-noise and combined.

4. Compare: Blink, Difference (each visit minus the others, so still stars vanish), Change map (one picture of everything that changed) and Deep stack. Gaia DR3 stars are moved to each visit's date, so a moving object with no Gaia match stands out and is listed as a candidate.

5. Measure: click an object and Galadriel follows it across visits and fits its motion, finds the camera where it is brightest, and builds its spectrum (each SPHEREx picture samples a different wavelength) and light curve. For stars too bright for the detector, it measures the glow around the core.

PROOF IT WORKS

Run on real SPHEREx data for all five challenge targets, measuring from SPHEREx alone:

- Barnard's Star: 9.8″/yr (catalogue 10.4)

- WISE 0855: 11.1″/yr (catalogue 8.2), visible only in the 4.4–5 µm camera

- Epsilon Indi B: 4.4″/yr (catalogue 4.7)

- RW Aurigae and R Draconis: correctly reported as not moving; R Draconis's 12 visits show its brightness rising and falling.

Every error is under one SPHEREx pixel (6.2″). The full table is inside the app ("Does it work?").

WHO IT IS FOR AND ITS IMPACT

Students, teachers, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists as well as professionals. The expert console is the default; four one-minute guided missions on real data, a numbered page map, a plain-language briefing under the image and an "i" explanation on every panel teach newcomers as they go. The interface works in 10 languages: English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Sinhala and Tamil, so students in Sri Lanka and around the world can use it in their own language. Findings can be shared as a link or embedded in another web page.

CREATIVITY

A spacecraft-console interface with switch sounds and a five-step mission checklist (Acquire, Observe, Detect, Analyse, Report). Choosing one of SPHEREx's 102 colours reveals objects that broadband viewers miss: the coldest known brown dwarf only appears in the longest-wavelength camera.

RELIABILITY

The five challenge targets are bundled with the app, so they open in under a second and keep working when the archive is down (this happened repeatedly during the hackathon). The tool queries IRSA's live tables, so new SPHEREx data releases appear without code changes.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Astroquery; JavaScript and HTML Canvas (no frameworks), Web Audio; Docker, hosted on Render. Open source: https://github.com/Shebulan-Joshwel/galadriel
